validator_note: Aggregated from per-stage JSONs stage-1 through stage-6; cross-stage inconsistencies identified via grep of stages-validated/ markdown corpus. Stage 6 has a minor internal discrepancy: total_claims=84 in structured JSON header but gate_reasoning references 98 claims — 84 used throughout as it matches the claim array length.

corpus_claims_low.stage_4_flag: Stage 4 solo L-rate is 69.4% (84/121), just below the 70% re-run threshold. It is the single weakest stage in the corpus and is the primary driver of the corpus-level L rate.

corpus_unique_domains.citation_diversity_grade_reasoning: 328 unique domains far exceeds the 40-60 ship threshold. The diversity grade would be 'ship' on domain count alone — however the domain diversity metric is misleading here because (a) 15 domains appear in 3+ stages indicating structural source reuse, (b) freightwaves.com appears across all 6 stages as a catch-all relay for vendor statistics, (c) five secondary-market-research aggregator domains (mordorintelligence, marketsandmarkets, gminsights, grandviewresearch, precedenceresearch) appear in 3-4 stages each and all receive automatic L overrides, and (d) 94 of the 328 unique domains are vendor or vendor-adjacent sites that add volume without adding source quality. Adjusted quality-weighted domain diversity is estimated at 110-130 truly independent sources — still above the 40-60 ship target but the raw 328 overstates diversity.

top_overused_sources.issue: Appears in every stage as primary relay for vendor statistics, regulatory events, and market trends. Not itself a primary source — it is named-author trade press at best, vendor-narrative relay at worst. Dozens of L-confidence claims across stages source their only URL to FreightWaves articles re-quoting vendor data. When FreightWaves is the sole citation for a quantified claim, single-trade-source override applies.

Used as catch-all citation for vendor press releases across all stages. GlobeNewswire is a press release distribution wire — it does not independently verify or editorially review claims. It does NOT add source quality above the underlying vendor press release. Multiple stages treat GlobeNewswire as a named-author trade publication when it is a distribution channel. This has inflated M-confidence scores in stages 1, 2, 3, and 4 where GlobeNewswire is cited as the 'second source' to elevate from L to M.

Same issue as globenewswire.com — press release distribution wire mistaken for trade press in several claims. PRNewswire is the publisher-of-record for corporate press releases; it does not editorially validate content. Used across stages 1, 3, 4, 5, 6.

FTV Capital is the venture investor in Highway (Stage 1, Stage 2). The $500M-$700M freight fraud annual loss figure — which is the single most-cited cross-stage cost figure in stages 1 and 2 — originates from FTV Capital's Highway investment thesis. It is an L-confidence single-vendor-source claim, and should not be treated as an industry baseline figure in any downstream synthesis. Confirmed as the same source in both stages.
top_overused_sources.special_flag: This is the origin of the $500M-$700M figure that propagates across stages 1 and 2 with L confidence. Its recurrence inflates the apparent cost-of-fraud estimate for the freight broker segment.

top_overused_sources.issue: Secondary-market-research firm. Appears in stages 1, 3, 4, 6 — always triggering the secondary-market-research override (automatic L for market sizing). The ASEAN road freight $119.43B figure (stage 1), fleet telematics market figures (stage 3), RTTVP market sizing (stage 4), and parametric insurance market (stage 6) all originate here. Cross-stage dependency: if Mordor's methodology is wrong, it distorts four separate TAM/market-sizing arguments.

Unaudited private-company revenue database. Used in stages 2 and 4 for private company revenue figures (Haulio ARR, project44 revenue). Latka's methodology is not independently audited; it relies on CEO interviews and AI estimation. Creates a specific cross-stage inconsistency: project44 revenue is cited as ~$210M in stage-4-value-chain.md (Latka estimate) and ~$175M ARR in stage-4-pain-points.md (different Latka figure from same database) — both from the same source, neither audited.

cross_stage_inconsistencies.topic: project44 revenue — two figures from same source in same stage
cross_stage_inconsistencies.claim_1: project44 FY2024 revenue estimated ~$210M (Latka estimate, VC-3)
cross_stage_inconsistencies.claim_2: project44 ~$175M ARR by end-2024 (Latka estimate, footnote 6)
cross_stage_inconsistencies.source_overlap: Both figures cite getlatka.com — same unaudited database, different figures. $210M vs $175M ARR is a $35M discrepancy from the same source, suggesting Latka's estimate changed between query dates or Latka uses a different revenue definition (GAAP vs ARR) for the two pages.
cross_stage_inconsistencies.resolution: Remove one figure. Stage-4-value-chain.md VC-3 notes this as 'estimated'; pain-points footnote 6 uses it as fact. Both should be qualified as 'Latka estimate, unaudited'. The company's own press release confirms only '>30% YoY growth' without stating a revenue starting point — $175M and $210M cannot both be correct.
cross_stage_inconsistencies.impact: Stage 4 is the only stage with zero H-confidence claims. This inconsistency is the most visible data quality issue in the corpus.

cross_stage_inconsistencies.topic: Indonesia commercial vehicle fleet count — three different figures across stages
cross_stage_inconsistencies.claim_1: Indonesia has 4M+ registered commercial vehicles (no source cited, bare assertion, claim VC-40, L confidence)
cross_stage_inconsistencies.claim_2: Total SEA commercial vehicle fleet in Indonesia exceeds 23M (Mordor Intelligence, L confidence). Stage 3 value chain data table corrects this to 6,091,822 registered trucks (BPS Indonesia 2023, H confidence) and notes the 23M Mordor figure likely covers all non-motorcycle vehicles.
cross_stage_inconsistencies.claim_3: Cartrack 274k devices vs. total addressable commercial vehicle fleet in SEA 'exceeds 23M in Indonesia alone' — reuses Mordor figure despite BPS correction in same document
cross_stage_inconsistencies.source_overlap: Stage 3 contains an internal contradiction: it both corrects the 23M figure to 6.09M (BPS, H confidence) AND continues to use the 23M figure in narrative context. Stage 1 uses a third figure (4M+) with no source. The three figures (4M, 6.09M, 23M) appear across two stages.
cross_stage_inconsistencies.resolution: Use only the BPS Indonesia figure (6,091,822 trucks, 2023) as the authoritative baseline. Remove 4M+ from Stage 1 (source it to BPS or remove). Remove 23M references from Stage 3 narrative and substitute BPS truck count. The 23M figure may refer to all road motor vehicles excluding motorcycles per Mordor's methodology — if used at all, it must be clearly qualified.
cross_stage_inconsistencies.impact: Indonesia fleet size is cited in stages 1, 3, and 4 as a market-sizing anchor for telematics, carrier vetting, and RTTVP opportunity. The three-figure discrepancy (4M vs 6.09M vs 23M) makes the SEA market size argument inconsistent across stages.

cross_stage_inconsistencies.topic: $500M-$700M freight fraud annual loss figure — cross-stage propagation of L-confidence VC-estimate
cross_stage_inconsistencies.claim_1: $500M-$700M in freight fraud payment losses annually (ftvcapital.com, L confidence)
cross_stage_inconsistencies.claim_2: $500M-$700M annual freight payment fraud losses (ftvcapital.com + freightwaves.com, L confidence)

cross_stage_inconsistencies.topic: Strategic cargo theft 1,475% growth — consistent figure, inconsistent attribution
cross_stage_inconsistencies.observation: The 1,475% strategic theft growth figure appears in three stages. In Stage 1 it is attributed to CargoNet/Verisk. In Stage 4 it cites 'FreightWaves April 2025' citing CargoNet. In Stage 5 it cites 'CargoNet/FreightWaves'. The underlying data is consistent (H confidence from Verisk CargoNet), but the citation chains differ — Stage 4 adds an FBI/IC3 PSA as a second corroborating source (IC3.gov), which is a material improvement. Stages 1 and Stage 5 do not carry this FBI corroboration.
cross_stage_inconsistencies.resolution: Add FBI IC3 April 2026 PSA citation (https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260430) as a secondary corroborating source in Stages 1 and 5 wherever the 1,475% figure appears. This is a harmless upgrade — the underlying data is correct and Stage 4 already validated this citation path.
cross_stage_inconsistencies.impact: Low — the figure itself is credible, the inconsistency is in citation completeness not in the claim value.

cross_stage_redundancies.description: Overhaul is profiled substantively in four separate stages: carrier fraud detection (stage 1), in-transit visibility (stage 4), cargo security (stage 5), and cargo insurance/claims (stage 6). The $5B cargo recovered claim, $105M Series C, and SensiGuard acquisition appear in stages 4, 5, and 6 with slightly different citation specificity. The stage-5 citation (freightwaves.com + stocktitan.net) is the most complete. Stage-6 VC-Overhaul-3 cites the same series C as $105M. Recommend consolidating Overhaul's full profile into the stage where it is most central (Stage 5 — cargo security) and cross-referencing in other stages rather than re-profiling.
cross_stage_redundancies.redundant_claim_overlap: Series C $105M appears in stages 4 (indirectly via VC-28), 5 (VC-13), and 6 (referenced in VC-Reliance context). SensiGuard acquisition appears in stages 5 and 6.

cross_stage_redundancies.description: TIA April 2025 survey data (1,611 Watchdog reports, average $402K loss, 97% truckload fraud mode, 83% experienced 3+ fraud types, 65% increase in reports) is cited in both stages 1 and 2 with H/M confidence correctly applied. This is appropriate cross-citation of a primary source — it is not a quality problem, but downstream synthesis should treat these as the same dataset, not two independent measurements of fraud frequency.
cross_stage_redundancies.redundant_claim_overlap: TIA April 2025 report cited in PP-1.1, PP-1.1-cost-5, PP-1.1-freq-4, PP-1.1-cost-6 (stage 1) and PP2.1-cost-2, PP2.1-freq-2, PP2.4-freq-2, PP2.5-freq-1 (stage 2). Recommend adding a cross-reference note in stage 2 to direct readers to stage 1's fuller treatment.

five_top_highest_confidence_findings.finding: US/Canada cargo theft reached record levels in 2024-2025: 3,625 incidents and $454.9M in losses in 2024 (27% YoY increase); escalating to 2,646 confirmed thefts and ~$725M estimated losses in 2025 (+36% in average theft value to $273,990). Strategic theft (fraud-enabled) grew 1,475% from Q1 2022 to Q4 2024.
primary_sources: FBI IC3 PSA April 2026 (ic3.gov) — corroborates strategic theft trajectory
five_top_highest_confidence_findings.commercial_significance: The cargo theft problem is demonstrably worsening and the causal mechanism is strategy-based fraud (not opportunistic) — validating the need for counterparty risk and carrier vetting tools.

five_top_highest_confidence_findings.finding: TIA April 2025 primary survey of member freight brokers: average company lost $402,344/year to fraud; 22% lost more than $200K in a single six-month period; 83% experienced three or more distinct fraud types in six months; 97% cited truckload as the most fraud-prone mode; TIA Watchdog recorded 1,611 fraud reports in a six-month window (Sep 2024-Feb 2025), a 65% increase over the prior comparable period.
primary_sources: TIA State of Fraud in the Industry April 2025 (news.tianet.org) — primary industry association survey
five_top_highest_confidence_findings.commercial_significance: The TIA survey is the corpus's single best source for quantifying the frequency and financial impact of freight fraud at the freight broker level — independent of any vendor's commercial interest.

five_top_highest_confidence_findings.finding: Platform financial health risk is real and quantified: Uber Freight posted EBITDA loss of $(22)M on $1.28B gross bookings in FY2024; GoGoX (HKEX-listed) recorded a 12.3% revenue decline in FY2024 to RMB 660.1M with negative EBITDA of RMB 68.3M; Full Truck Alliance (NYSE:YMM) is the outlier with RMB 11.24B revenue (+33.2%) and RMB 3.12B net income.
primary_sources: Uber Technologies SEC earnings press release (investor.uber.com)
five_top_highest_confidence_findings.commercial_significance: Public-company disclosures confirm structural financial fragility in digital freight platforms outside China, validated by the Convoy collapse case study. Shippers face concentration risk when selecting digital platform partners.

five_top_highest_confidence_findings.finding: SEA logistics infrastructure quality is measurably inferior to peer markets: World Bank LPI 2023 ranks Singapore 1st globally, Malaysia 31st, Thailand 37th, Indonesia 61st (down from 45th in 2018). Indonesia's decline in rank over five years is a primary-multilateral-confirmed signal of logistics system deterioration, not a trend artifact.
five_top_highest_confidence_findings.commercial_significance: The LPI data provides a defensible, independent benchmark for the gap between SEA logistics maturity and the infrastructure assumed by North American-originated logistics risk management tools.

five_top_highest_confidence_findings.finding: Global marine cargo insurance market was $22.64B in gross written premium in 2024 (IUMI primary-association data); SEA country-level data available at primary level: Indonesia (AAUI) and Malaysia (PIAM) both publish country marine cargo GWP. The Vesttoo fraud case (fraudulent LoC collateral in a reinsurance sidecar structure) is documented via Artemis.bm and legal proceedings — a primary-level anchor for systemic counterparty risk in cargo insurance markets.
five_top_highest_confidence_findings.commercial_significance: Stage 6 has the strongest primary source mix in the corpus. The marine cargo market size, SEA country insurance data, and Vesttoo counterparty risk event are all defensible with primary sources.

three_top_questions_for_field_validation.question: What is the actual per-carrier manual vetting labor cost for a mid-size SEA 3PL, and what hourly rate applies to logistics coordinators in Singapore and Kuala Lumpur?
three_top_questions_for_field_validation.why_critical: The SEA commercial opportunity in Stage 1 rests on the $24K-$216K annual vetting cost estimate (ASSUMED-2). This is the most commercially consequential ASSUMED tag in the corpus — it underlies the unit economics argument for the SEA carrier vetting tool opportunity. Without a primary labor cost anchor, the SEA pain-point economic case is unverifiable.
three_top_questions_for_field_validation.evidence_needed: MOM Singapore Occupational Wage Statistics (logistics/operations coordinator role), DOSM Malaysia Salaries and Wages Survey, or a Mercer/Korn Ferry SEA Logistics Salary Benchmark for the relevant job family. One survey source is sufficient to replace the assumption.

three_top_questions_for_field_validation.question: What is the actual adoption rate of telematics-based underwriting among commercial trucking insurers in North America and SEA, and do insurers systematically request telematics data at policy renewal?
three_top_questions_for_field_validation.why_critical: Three separate claims across Stages 3 and 6 rely on telematics-sharing statistics that originate from carrier management trade press or insurer marketing (88% of fleets have telematics; only 64% share it for underwriting; 79% say insurers never asked). These figures underpin the 'telematics as risk signal' thesis in Stage 6 and the 'data silos' framing in Stage 3. None has a named survey methodology or primary-association backing.

For SEA: direct insurer interviews (Chubb, Tokio Marine, Allianz Commercial) on whether telematics data is solicited or accepted for commercial motor pricing.

three_top_questions_for_field_validation.question: What is the universe of uninsured or underinsured small shippers globally, and is the 60-70% of global freight being under-insured a defensible market-sizing claim?
three_top_questions_for_field_validation.why_critical: The 70 million uninsured shipper figure and the 60%+ uninsured freight estimate (Stage 6) are the headline market opportunity claims for the cargo insurance digitization thesis. Both originate from Loadsure's marketing materials and have no independent primary anchor. These figures are central to the commercial case for insurtech/parametric cargo insurance products in Stage 6.
three_top_questions_for_field_validation.evidence_needed: ITC (International Trade Centre) SME Trade Finance reports; World Bank Global Findex for SME insurance penetration; ICC/SWIFT Trade Register for trade finance exposure and insurance take-up rates; UNCTAD World Investment Report; IUMI sub-data on cargo insurance penetration as a share of global trade value (IUMI is already cited in Stage 6 at H confidence — check whether IUMI publishes penetration estimates alongside GWP data).

final_gate_threshold_applied: 53.2% Low-confidence claims — within the 30-70% ship-with-flag band
gate_reasoning: The corpus of 568 scored claims across six stages produces 79 High (13.9%), 187 Medium (32.9%), and 302 Low (53.2%) confidence scores. The 53.2% Low rate places the full corpus firmly in the ship-with-flag band. All six individual stages also received ship-with-flag gate decisions. The corpus CANNOT be upgraded to ship-as-is because: (1) Stage 4 (In-transit visibility) has zero High-confidence claims and a 69.4% Low rate — it is one percentage point from the re-run threshold and contains a confirmed factual error (project44 revenue internal inconsistency). (2) Stage 3 contains a confirmed factual error (Nirvana Series D round size) that must be corrected before any external use. (3) The corpus's primary SEA commercial opportunity argument rests on three ASSUMED tags (SEA labor cost, ASEAN freight market size, SEA digital penetration rates) that remain unresolved after deep research. (4) The $500M-$700M fraud loss figure — the most-cited cross-stage cost claim — remains a single-vendor L-confidence estimate that should not anchor any commercial or investment conclusion. The corpus SHOULD be shipped for internal research orientation because: the High-confidence core is strong (TIA primary survey, Verisk CargoNet, World Bank LPI, public company SEC/HKEX filings, IUMI marine insurance statistics, TAPA/ReCAAP incident data) and correctly anchors the most material factual claims across the five strongest stages (1, 2, 3, 5, 6). Stage 5 and Stage 6 both have High-confidence claims exceeding 20% of their total, indicating credible primary-source coverage of the security and insurance domains. The research is structurally sound as a stage-by-stage value chain analysis; it is not suitable for direct client-facing citation without the flags and field validation items identified above.
